KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and unseasonably mild again today. Highs in the 
60s.

Large high pressure slowly shifts east of the region today. 
Nonetheless...still expect plenty of sunshine today and with 925T 
near +10C. This should result in another day with highs in the 60s. 
Winds will be rather light too...so a great day is in store for late 
November standards. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... Widespread heavy rain later Sun into early Mon am 
with an axis of 1-3". Brief nuisance poor drainage street flooding 
possible...but the progressive nature of the system will likely 
prevent significant impacts. Splashover/Very Minor coastal 
flooding possible, but no significant impacts expected. Most of
Mon will be dry and unseasonably mild with highs in the 60s.

The models have come into much better agreement in robust southern 
stream energy resulting in a developing low pressure system off the 
southeast coast today and tonight. This will combined with another 
piece of shortwave energy that carves out a trough over the Great 
Lakes Sun...which amplifies the upper level flow along the east 
coast. This will force this intensifying low pressure system to 
rapidly lift northward along the coast. The models are in much 
better agreement in the track of this intensifying low pressure
system...which should pass in the vicinity of the Cape/Islands 
very late Sunday night. However...there are still some 
differences which will impact the axis of the heaviest rain. 
While this will be a very fast moving low pressure 
system...given its origins on the sub- tropical jet it is loaded
in moisture. Pwats reach 3-4 standard deviations above normal. 
So despite the fast moving system...we are thinking an axis of 
1-3" of rain occurs in a relatively short period of time. As 
mentioned...there are still differences in the axis of heaviest 
QPF. It appears that the heaviest rain will be east of the CT 
River to near the I-95 corridor...But leaving the option open 
for this axis to shift a bit further east or west. We may see 
some showers arrive by late Sun afternoon...But the bulk of the 
heavy rain will be Sunday night and already ending by early Mon 
morning. In fact...the bulk of the heavy rain will have exited 
the coast by the morning rush hour. Some brief urban/street 
flooding is possible...but the progressive nature of this system
will likely prevent significant impacts. And as mentioned...the
bulk of the rain will exit the region by the peak of the Mon am
rush hour. In fact...Mon should mainly be a dry and very mild 
day with highs well into the 60s.
 
As for winds...we should see a period of gusty winds along the coast 
Sunday night with a 925 mb southeast LLJ of 55-65 knots. While there 
is an inversion...still expect southeast wind gusts of 25 to 45 mph 
along the coast with the strongest of those winds near the Cape and 
Islands. And given the limited wind risk...thinking that any coastal 
flooding/splashover during Monday/s high tide should be rather minor 
with a limited impact along the eastern MA coast/Cape and Nantucket.
Basically just looking at some splashover/very minor coastal flooding.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Dry & much colder weather follows Tue into Wed with 
highs in the 40s. Lows Tue night mainly in the upper teens & 20s. 

Behind this departing coastal storm...dry but colder temperatures 
will work into southern New England. Cold advection should keep high 
temps mainly in the 40s Tue and Wed with perhaps some of the high 
terrain remaining in the upper 30s. High pressure overhead will keep 
us dry too and setup Tue night to be an ideal night of radiational 
cooling. Lows Tue night will probably be mainly in the upper teens 
and 20s with even downtown Boston likely dropping into the lower 
30s. Probably the coldest weather of the season for many
locations.

KEY MESSAGE 4...Potential for an impactful Nor'easter late Wed night 
into Thanksgiving. Ptype favors mainly rain...but a bit of snow/ice 
is possible at the onset across the interior. Strong winds are 
possible along the coast and we  are concerned for coastal flooding 
given very high astro tides. Significant marine impact possible
too.

Although still quite the ways in the future...the long term guidance 
is in very good agreement that another robust piece of southern 
stream energy will try to interact with northern stream energy. The 
long range guidance indicates this may develop into a Nor'easter and 
impact our region late Wed night into Thanksgiving. Ptype looks to 
be mainly rain...But antecedent airmass may be just cold enough for 
a bit of snow/ice at the onset across the interior.

This system actually has the potential to be more impactful than 
what we are expecting late Sunday into early Mon morning for a 
couple of reasons. The first is that this will be associated with an 
initial 1040 mb high over the Canadian Maritimes. That means the 
potential for strong winds along the coast will be much higher than
